questions.question: What is an API Gateway?

options.text: A server that acts as a single entry point for API requests, handling routing, authentication, and other cross-cutting concerns

questions.explanation: API Gateway: reverse proxy for APIs. Single entry point. Handles: routing, authentication, rate limiting, caching, request transformation, monitoring. Decouples clients from backend services.

questions.question: What are the main responsibilities of an API Gateway?
questions.explanation: API Gateway responsibilities: routing (direct to correct service), security (auth, SSL termination), traffic management (rate limiting, throttling), transformation (request/response modification), observability (logging, metrics).

questions.question: How does an API Gateway help with microservices?

options.text: Provides single entry point, hides internal service topology, handles cross-cutting concerns centrally

questions.explanation: Microservices + Gateway: clients see one endpoint (not dozens of services), internal changes don't affect clients, centralized auth/rate limiting/monitoring. Essential for managing microservices complexity.

questions.question: What is the difference between an API Gateway and a load balancer?

options.text: Load balancer: distributes traffic; API Gateway: application-level concerns (auth, routing, transformation)

questions.explanation: Load balancer: L4/L7 traffic distribution, health checks, simple routing. API Gateway: application-aware, authentication, rate limiting, request transformation, API versioning. Often used together.

questions.question: What is request transformation in an API Gateway?

options.text: Modifying requests/responses (headers, body, format) between client and backend

questions.explanation: Request transformation: modify before forwarding. Examples: add headers, change JSON to XML, rename fields, aggregate responses from multiple services. Enables: backend changes without client changes, protocol translation.

questions.question: What is API composition in an API Gateway?

options.text: Aggregating responses from multiple backend services into a single response

questions.explanation: API composition: client makes one request, gateway calls multiple services, combines responses. Reduces client complexity, fewer round trips. Example: product page needs data from product, inventory, reviews services.

questions.question: What are popular API Gateway solutions?
questions.explanation: API Gateway options: AWS API Gateway (managed), Kong (open source, enterprise), NGINX (reverse proxy + gateway), Apigee (Google), Azure API Management, Traefik, Ambassador. Choose based on needs.

questions.question: What is the potential downside of an API Gateway?

options.text: Single point of failure, added latency, can become a bottleneck

questions.explanation: Gateway risks: SPOF (need HA deployment), latency (extra hop), bottleneck (all traffic through it), complexity (another component to manage). Mitigate: redundancy, caching, proper sizing.

questions.question: What is SSL/TLS termination at the API Gateway?

options.text: Decrypting HTTPS traffic at the gateway, forwarding plain HTTP to backends

questions.explanation: SSL termination: gateway handles HTTPS, backends receive HTTP. Benefits: offload crypto from backends, centralize certificate management. Consideration: internal traffic unencrypted (use mTLS or private network).

questions.question: How does an API Gateway handle API versioning?

options.text: Routes requests to different backend versions based on URL path, header, or query parameter

questions.explanation: API versioning via gateway: /v1/users → service-v1, /v2/users → service-v2. Or by header: Accept-Version: v2. Gateway routes appropriately. Enables: running multiple versions, gradual migration.

questions.question: What is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern related to API Gateways?

options.text: Separate API Gateways optimized for different client types (web, mobile, IoT)

questions.explanation: BFF: separate gateway per client type. Web BFF: optimized for browser. Mobile BFF: optimized for mobile (smaller payloads, different aggregations). Each tailored to client needs. Avoids one-size-fits-all.

questions.question: A company has 50 microservices. Clients currently call services directly. What problem does this cause?

options.text: Clients must know all service locations, handle auth for each, complex client code

questions.explanation: Direct calls problem: clients coupled to service topology, auth logic duplicated, no central rate limiting, hard to change backends. Solution: API Gateway as single entry point, handles cross-cutting concerns.
